Tidal Patterns in Coastal Estuaries

By A. Fieldworker

Estuaries sit where a river meets the sea, and the water in them is never quite one thing or the other. Twice a day the tide pushes salt water upstream, and twice a day it drains away again, leaving behind a gradient that shifts hour by hour. Anything living there has to tolerate that swing, which is why estuarine species tend to be generalists rather than specialists, and why a survey taken at dawn can differ sharply from one taken at dusk.

Measuring the gradient is harder than it sounds. A single probe lowered from a jetty reports the salinity at one point, at one depth, at one moment, and none of those three things stay fixed for long. Fresh water is lighter than salt water, so it rides on top rather than mixing evenly, and a probe a metre lower may read something else entirely. Field teams usually take a vertical profile instead, stepping the instrument down through the column.

UNIQUEHEADINGDELTA

The pattern repeats with the lunar cycle. Spring tides, which arrive when the sun and moon pull together, push the salt wedge further upstream than neap tides do. Over a month the boundary migrates several kilometres in each direction, and the species living along that stretch shift with it, tracking conditions rather than holding position.

  • Surface readings taken hourly across a full tidal cycle
  • Vertical profiles at half-metre intervals
  • Reference samples from the river mouth and the upstream limit

A useful rule of thumb is that the wedge advances until the river's outflow balances the tide's push. In a dry season the river weakens and the salt reaches further inland; after heavy rain it is driven back toward the sea within a day or two. Long records therefore say more about rainfall than about the tide itself, which is why the two are logged together. See RELATIVELINKEPSILON for the full protocol.
